extracted.intended_audience: registered patent attorneys and other practitioners before the USPTO, and attorneys/respondents facing reciprocal discipline under USPTO rules
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria the USPTO applies when deciding whether to impose reciprocal discipline based on a State court's disciplinary adjudication under 37 C.F.R. § 11.24. Covers the legal presumptions, defenses (Selling elements), due process requirements, proof standards, and typical misconduct (e.g., misappropriation) that warrant disbarment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal discipline presumption (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Director shall impose the identical public censure, public reprimand, probation, disbarment, suspension, or disciplinary disqualification unless the practitioner clearly and convincingly demonstrates, and the USPTO Director finds there is a genuine issue of material fact that one of the listed defenses applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text of the regulation is quoted on the page; practitioner must meet the high 'clear and convincing' standard to prevent imposition of identical discipline. This is the starting presumption: a state disbarment creates a federal-level presumption that identical discipline is proper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selling v. Radford standard / burden of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Selling v. Radford, state disbarment creates a federal-level presumption that imposition of reciprocal disbarment is proper, and it is the respondent attorney's burden to demonstrate, by clear and convincing evidence, that one of the Selling elements precludes reciprocal discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal jurisprudence cited (Selling, In re Kramer, In re Friedman, In re Zdravkovich) emphasizes narrow review; the USPTO (like federal courts) is not sitting as a court of review to discover errors in state proceedings. The respondent must prove a Selling element by clear and convincing evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selling element (i): Deprivation of due process
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciprocal discipline may be defeated if 'the procedure elsewhere was so lacking in notice or opportunity to be heard as to constitute deprivation of due process.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To meet this defense, respondent must clearly and convincingly show lack of notice or meaningful opportunity to be heard. Page cites Mathews v. Eldridge and case law explaining due process in disciplinary proceedings: reasonable notice, ability to participate, present evidence, testify, cross-examine, be represented by counsel, and object to findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due process requirements in attorney disciplinary proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Due process requires 'the opportunity to be heard at a meaningful time and in a meaningful manner'—reasonable notice of charges and meaningful hearings where the attorney can present evidence, testify, cross-examine witnesses, and make argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authorities (In re Karten, In re Ruffalo, In re Squire, In re Zdravkovich, Ginger v. Circuit Court) establish that participation in hearings, representation by counsel, depositions, ability to cross-examine and to present witnesses satisfy due process. Mere disagreement with state conclusions does not establish deprivation of due process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selling element (ii): Infirmity of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciprocal discipline may be defeated if 'there was such infirmity of proof establishing the conduct as to give rise to the clear conviction that the Office could not, consistently with its duty, accept as final the conclusion on that subject.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The standard is difficult to meet: respondent must show an infirmity of proof so serious that federal acceptance of the state finding would be inconsistent with USPTO's duty. Deference is given to trier-of-fact credibility determinations; mere disagreement with findings is insufficient. (Citations: In re Zdravkovich and other cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Selling element (iii): Grave injustice
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciprocal discipline may be defeated if 'the imposition of the same public censure, public reprimand, probation, disbarment, suspension or disciplinary disqualification by the Office would result in a grave injustice.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysis focuses on whether the severity of the state-ordered punishment 'fits' the misconduct (proportionality). Courts inquire whether the sanction imposed by the state was so ill-fitted to the adjudicated misconduct that imposing the same sanction would produce a grave injustice. Case examples illustrate that sanctions within the appropriate range do not constitute grave injustice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selling element (iv): Practitioner was not publicly disciplined
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciprocal discipline may be defeated if the practitioner can argue that he or she was not publicly censured, publicly reprimanded, placed on probation, disbarred, suspended or disciplinarily disqualified by the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a procedural/technical ground: if the practitioner shows the state did not actually impose public discipline of the sort claimed, reciprocal discipline should not be imposed. The practitioner still bears the clear-and-convincing evidentiary burden to prove this.

rubrics_metrics.name: State licensure confers disciplinary jurisdiction regardless of location of misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: A lawyer admitted to practice in a jurisdiction is subject to that jurisdiction's disciplinary authority regardless of where the lawyer's conduct occurs (citing Middlesex, ABA Model Rule 8.5, New Jersey Rule 8.5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Licensure in the state provides authority to discipline for conduct occurring elsewhere; ignorance of the scope of disciplinary jurisdiction is not an excuse. The Office rejects claims that misconduct occurring in another state deprives the licensing state of jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deference to state fact-finding; narrow scope of federal review
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office (and federal courts) will not act as a court of review to reweigh evidence; determinations of credibility and factual findings by the state tribunal generally receive deference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Zdravkovich and other authority: petitioner faces a narrow standard — must establish one of the Selling elements by clear and convincing evidence to displace deference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misappropriation of client funds as particularly egregious misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowingly misappropriating client funds, failing to segregate disputed funds, and related conduct constitute serious professional misconduct that typically results in disbarment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The New Jersey Supreme Court and cited precedent state that misappropriation of trust funds 'almost invariably results in disbarment' and is among the most egregious acts; mitigating factors rarely override the requirement of disbarment. The Order cites specific rule violations (RPC 1.15(a) knowing misappropriation; RPC 1.15(c) failing to segregate disputed funds; RPC 1.5(c) failing to provide an accounting; RPC 1.15(d) and Rule 1:21-6 recordkeeping; RPC 8.4(d) conduct prejudicial to administration of justice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct supporting disbarment: concealment and failure to account
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberate deposit of unauthorized fees into accounts to conceal or disavow control, transfer of funds out of jurisdiction to avoid recovery, and failure to comply with court orders to return funds or provide an accounting support findings of knowing misappropriation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order summarizes factual behaviors (e.g., transferring funds to relatives' trusts, wiring funds to China, failing to return funds despite orders) that illustrate types of acts the state found sufficient to support disbarment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionality analysis for 'grave injustice' (sanction fit to misconduct)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether imposing the same discipline would be a 'grave injustice' depends on whether the sanction is within the appropriate range of penalties for the adjudicated misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited cases (In re Thav, In re Kramer, In re Attorney Discipline Matter, Matter of Benjamin) illustrate the proportionality inquiry: if the state's sanction is within the normal range for the offense, reciprocal imposition is not a grave injustice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of proof to avoid reciprocal discipline: clear and convincing evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevent imposition of the reciprocal exclusion, the respondent must demonstrate one of the Selling criteria by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple authorities cited reinforce that the respondent bears this burden and that it is a demanding standard; unsupported allegations or mere disagreement with findings do not meet it.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO-imposed consequences and required actions upon exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: If excluded, the practitioner will be removed from practice before the USPTO and must comply with specific obligations: publication of notice, notice to disciplinary agencies, compliance with 37 C.F.R. § 11.58 duties, dissociation from Customer Numbers and PKI, prohibition on obtaining or being added to a Customer Number until reinstated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Order lists mandatory actions: exclude from practice; publish a Notice in the Official Gazette; notify state disciplinary agencies and courts; comply with duties under 37 C.F.R. § 11.58; dissociate and disable USPTO Customer Numbers/PKI; do not apply for or obtain a USPTO Customer Number until reinstatement. Also provides right to judicial review under 35 U.S.C. § 32 within 30 days.
